finding.claim: reset_password_loose accepts a reset token via PHP loose == comparison, so type-juggled or empty tokens can match a stored NULL/empty or numeric-string token and reset the account password.
finding.source: $token parameter supplied by caller (request input per reset flow; no caller in repo)
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (reset.php:5-6)

trace.note: Loads stored token for $email via quoted query; fetch() returns first row
$row['token'] == $token: loose comparison, no type check on $token, no empty/NULL check on stored token
On match, password replaced with password_hash($new)

finding.guards_checked: $db->quote on email (SQLi not reachable); row existence check; no null/empty check on stored token; no strict comparison; no expiry check

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is the row-existence test at reset.php:4 (`$row &&`), which is not a security control. The loose `==` at reset.php:4 has no strict comparison, type check, or empty/NULL check on $token or $row['token']. The sibling reset_password (reset.php:12-20) uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, which shows the safe form exists but is not applied here. No expiry check, and the query and UPDATE at reset.php:3, 5-6 are quoted via $db->quote, so SQL injection is not the issue.
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 uses loose `==` between the stored token and an unchecked $token, so a non-string $token such as boolean true (for example from a decoded JSON body) matches any non-empty stored token, and reset.php:5-6 then sets the password for that email. Caveat: no caller is in the repo, so the attacker's reachability (presumably anonymous via the reset flow) is inferred rather than shown; the "NULL/empty stored token" part of the claim is weaker than the boolean-juggling and magic-hash cases.

finding.claim: reset_password accepts an empty token when the stored token is NULL or empty, because hash_equals('', '') is true after the (string) cast, allowing a password reset without the token.
finding.source: $token parameter supplied by caller; attacker submits empty string
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... (reset.php:15-16)

trace.note: hash_equals($row['token'], (string)$token) returns true when both values are empty; no non-empty check on either side

finding.guards_checked: Constant-time hash_equals (prevents timing leak but not empty match); (string) cast; row existence check; $db->quote on email

verdict.guard_found: Only `$row &&` at reset.php:14 (row-existence check). It does not test that the stored token is non-empty. No other control is visible. The directory contains only reset.php, so there is no caller, schema, or token-generation code to show whether a resets row with NULL or empty token can exist.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: reset.php:13 loads the stored token, and reset.php:14 calls hash_equals($row['token'], (string)$token) with no non-empty check, so a NULL or '' stored token against an empty submitted token matches (NULL coerces to '' in coercive mode) and reset.php:15-16 then overwrites the password. Whether an anonymous attacker can reach that state depends on data and callers not in this directory (no code writes a resets row with an empty token, and no endpoint validates $token before line 14), so the exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never expired or consumed: the lookup has no expiry check, a successful reset does not delete or invalidate the token, and multiple outstanding tokens per email are all usable, so a leaked token remains a permanent password-reset credential.
finding.source: A previously issued reset token obtained by an attacker (leaked via logs, referrer, forwarded email, or shared link)

trace.note: SELECT token FROM resets WHERE email = ... with no expires_at/used filter and no ORDER BY; fetch() returns an arbitrary first row
Success returns true without deleting or marking the token used
Same lookup in reset_password, no expiry filter
Success returns true without invalidating the token

finding.guards_checked: Row existence check and constant-time compare in reset_password; no expiry, single-use, or invalidation logic visible in this file (may exist in schema or a cleanup job, not verified)

verdict.guard_found: reset.php:4 and :14 check the row exists and compare the token (loose == in reset_password_loose, hash_equals in reset_password). Nothing in reset.php checks expires_at or a used flag, and nothing deletes or invalidates the row after success (reset.php:7, :17). The only file in the directory is reset.php, so no schema or cleanup job is visible to rule out expiry elsewhere.
verdict.reason: The lookups at reset.php:3 and :13 have no expiry or used filter, and the success paths at reset.php:7 and :17 return true without deleting the token, so a leaked token stays usable for password reset until something outside this file removes it. The candidate overstates one point: fetch() at :3 and :13 returns a single row, so other outstanding tokens for the same email are not checked, and the "multiple tokens all usable" part of the claim is wrong. The core no-expiry, no-consume flaw still holds.
